Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Anna, a 40-year-old European data scientist, was on a consulting trip to a small Arab village in Jordan when she witnessed a sudden, violent explosion during a local festival. While on a tour bus with colleagues, a shell detonated in the distance, sending shock waves that rattled the bus, a plume of smoke, and flames that kissed the night sky. She saw the twisted bodies of villagers, heard their cries, and felt the heat of the fire on her face. The image of a woman being crushed, the crack of metal and the roar of flames were etched into her mind. The memory was not ordinary-it felt more vivid and real than any recollection of office meetings or data dashboards. Since that night, every sight of Arab architecture, the smell of spices, or even a brief flicker of a fire alarm in her office pulls her back into the scene. Those triggers drive her to throw herself into work; she overworks, spending long hours on data models to keep her mind occupied. She also ruminates, replaying the why of the event, convinced that she should have protected the people she saw. The sudden sense of threat from strangers-whether a passerby in the hallway or a colleague's casual greeting-only amplifies her fear. She repeatedly checks that her office door is locked, and when she hears footsteps in the corridor she freezes, convinced strangers pose a danger. Thus, the triggers lead her to maladaptive strategies, to heightened threat, and to harsh negative appraisals that she failed to protect those she watched. The intrusive memory of that night-its sharp sounds, bright flames, and relentless heat-surfaces without warning as Anna walks past a billboard or hears distant thunder. Each time the memory rushes back, she feels the sting of failure; she should have protected the villagers. That sense of failure feeds into the memory itself, making it feel even more real. The memory also fuels her rumination, which heightens the threat that strangers might approach, and amplifies her belief that the world is hostile. Each intrusive recall turns the scene into a fresh trigger, as the image of the burning village suddenly appears whenever she sees fire or a crowd. Thus the memory pushes her to overwork, to lock doors, and to remain hypervigilant. When she senses a stranger's approach, the threat she feels sharpens her resolve to keep busy. The panic leads her to double-check the office door, then sprint to her desk, where she will immediately immerse herself in spreadsheet data. This urge to avoid the perceived threat reinforces her pattern of overworking, while the repeated checking of locks and the heightened alertness keep her in a constant state of readiness, making ordinary movements feel like potential dangers. The threat, therefore, pushes her to overwork and to see ordinary moments as possible triggers. The endless cycle of overworking, checking, and rumination keeps the memory alive, and the memory keeps her locked in the same loop. Each new data model she builds feels like a shield against a possible blast, each lock she verifies a promise that no one can get close. In recent weeks, her marriage has become strained; her spouse, tired of her constant vigilance and excuses to work late, has begun to pull away. Anna's confidence has wavered; she has begun to question whether her life still has meaning. She now seeks help because the relentless cycle has left her exhausted and fearful that she might lose herself entirely. She hopes to find a way to let the past stay where it is-just a memory-so that she can reclaim her days and her sense of safety.
